bad: Could you give me a favor?
good: Could you do me a favor?
why: English uses the collocation “do someone a favor,” not “give someone a favor.” “Could you…” turns it into a polite request; you can follow it with the specific thing you need.
story: I was carrying a few boxes into the community room before our club meeting.
One box was awkward to lift while I held the door open.
My friend was nearby, so I asked, “Could you do me a favor?”
I explained that I needed help carrying the box inside.
They picked up the other side, and we moved it together.
I thanked them and set out the materials for the meeting.

good: I’ll wait for you outside.
why: In English, “wait” is followed by “for” before the person you are waiting for. The contraction “I’ll” also sounds natural when you are telling someone your immediate plan.
story: We agreed to meet near the entrance after work.
My friend texted that they needed a few more minutes.
I told them, “I’ll wait for you outside.”
I found a spot by the main doors and stayed out of the rain.
They arrived shortly afterward and waved when they saw me.
We walked to the café together.

good: I’m going home now.
why: “Home” can work as an adverb meaning “to the place where you live,” so it does not take “to” after “go.” Say “go to my home” only when you use “home” as a noun phrase, which is less common in this everyday context.
story: The movie had just ended, and it was getting late.
A few people in the group were deciding whether to find dessert.
I had an early start the next morning, so I said, “I’m going home now.”
My friend asked whether I wanted to share a ride.
We walked to the station together and checked the train times.
I sent a quick message when I got home.

bad: I didn’t see you for a long time.
good: I haven’t seen you in a long time.
why: The present perfect (“haven’t seen”) connects the past to now: the time apart began earlier and continues up to this meeting. “In a long time” is a common phrase in this greeting; the simple past would usually refer to a finished past period.
story: I ran into a former classmate at the weekend market.
We recognized each other near the fruit stand and stopped to talk.
I smiled and said, “I haven’t seen you in a long time.”
They told me they had moved to a neighborhood across town.
We caught up on work, friends, and the places we used to visit.
Before leaving, we exchanged numbers and made plans to meet again.

good: I’m running about ten minutes late.
why: English commonly uses “run late” to report that you are behind schedule. “About ten minutes” gives a useful estimate, while the present progressive describes the delay happening now.
story: Traffic slowed to a crawl on the way to dinner.
I checked the map and saw that the arrival time had moved back.
I texted my friend, “I’m running about ten minutes late.”
They replied that they would save me a seat.
I found parking a few minutes later and hurried inside.
We ordered drinks while we waited for the food.

good: I didn’t catch that.
why: “Listen” usually describes paying attention to sound; it does not mean that you failed to hear one particular sentence. “I didn’t catch that” is a common conversational way to say you missed what someone just said and invite them to repeat it.
story: The café was crowded, and the music was louder than usual.
My friend told me which table they had reserved.
I missed part of the sentence when a blender started.
I said, “I didn’t catch that. Which table did you say?”
They repeated the number, and I found the table near the window.
We sat down and continued our conversation.

good: Thanks for letting me know.
why: After “for,” use a noun or an -ing form, so “inform” would need to become “informing.” In this situation, “let me know” is the more conversational expression for giving someone useful information.
story: My neighbor messaged me that the building elevator would be out of service.
I had been planning to bring several heavy bags upstairs that evening.
I replied, “Thanks for letting me know.”
I changed my plan and picked up only what I could carry.
The next day, I used the stairs when I came home.
The early message saved me an inconvenient trip back to the lobby.

bad: Tell me when you will be free.
good: Let me know when you’re free.
why: “Tell me” is grammatical, but it can sound like a direct instruction. “Let me know” is a softer, common way to ask someone to contact you, and the present tense “you’re free” is natural in a time clause about a future situation.
story: I wanted to catch up with a friend who had a busy week.
We both had different work schedules, so choosing a time was difficult.
I wrote, “Let me know when you’re free.”
They checked their calendar after finishing a meeting.
Later, they suggested Saturday afternoon at a park nearby.
We picked a café to visit afterward.

good: I’ll be right back.
why: “Return” already means to come back, so adding “back” repeats the same idea. “I’ll be right back” is a familiar phrase when you expect to leave briefly and come back soon.
story: We were setting up snacks before guests arrived.
I noticed that we had run out of napkins.
I told my roommate, “I’ll be right back,” and walked to the corner shop.
The shop was only a few minutes away.
I bought napkins and a bottle of sparkling water.
When I returned, my roommate had finished arranging the plates.

good: Could I get a coffee, please?
why: “I want” is grammatically correct, but said directly to service staff it can sound like a blunt statement of demand. “Could I get…?” is a conventional, polite way to place an order; add the drink size or type if you need something specific.
story: I stopped at a café on my way to the train station.
There were a few people waiting, so I looked at the menu first.
When it was my turn, I said, “Could I get a coffee, please?”
The barista asked whether I wanted room for milk.
I answered and tapped my card at the counter.
I picked up the cup when my name was called.

bad: Do you have smaller size for this?
good: Do you have this in a smaller size?
why: “A smaller size” needs the article “a,” and English commonly uses “in a smaller size” to ask about another clothing size. Putting “this” first makes it clear which item you mean.
story: I found a jacket I liked while browsing a small shop.
The color was right, but the sleeves felt a little tight.
I asked the clerk, “Do you have this in a smaller size?”
They checked the stockroom and brought another one.
I tried it on and found that the fit was more comfortable.
I thanked the clerk and bought the jacket.

bad: Can you borrow me your charger?
good: Could I borrow your charger?
why: “Borrow” means to receive something temporarily; the person lending it is the one who lends it. Ask “Could I borrow…?” when you need to use someone else’s item, or “Could you lend me…?” when focusing on the other person.
story: My phone battery was almost empty while I was waiting for a ride.
A friend beside me had a charger in their bag.
I asked, “Could I borrow your charger?”
They handed it over and showed me the nearest outlet.
I charged my phone while we talked about the evening.
Before leaving, I unplugged it and gave it back.

good: Where’s the nearest bus stop?
why: Use “the” before “nearest” because you are asking about the closest stop in the area. “Where’s” is the natural contraction of “where is” in casual conversation; use the full form in more formal speech if you prefer.
story: I was visiting a neighborhood I had not been to before.
After leaving the bookstore, I wanted to take the bus back downtown.
I asked a person nearby, “Where’s the nearest bus stop?”
They pointed toward the corner and named the route I needed.
I thanked them and checked the bus sign before boarding.
The ride took me back to the central station.

bad: Does this bus go to downtown?
good: Does this bus go downtown?
why: “Downtown” commonly works as an adverb after “go,” so “to” is usually omitted in this question. “Go to downtown” is heard in some varieties and contexts, but “go downtown” is the usual phrasing in everyday American English.
story: I got on a bus after visiting a friend in the suburbs.
I was unsure whether the route continued toward the city center.
Before finding a seat, I asked the driver, “Does this bus go downtown?”
The driver confirmed that it stopped near the main library.
I sat by the window and watched for the landmark.
I got off at the right stop and walked the last few blocks.

good: Could you open the window, please?
why: The original is grammatically correct, but it is an imperative and can sound like an instruction. “Could you…?” frames the same action as a polite request, especially useful when you are asking rather than directing someone.
story: The afternoon sun warmed the room during our study session.
Everyone had been working quietly for nearly an hour.
I felt the air getting stuffy, so I asked, “Could you open the window, please?”
My classmate opened it a little to let in some fresh air.
A light breeze came through, and the room felt more comfortable.
We went back to our notes and finished the exercise.

bad: What do you want for eat?
good: What sounds good to you?
why: The original combines two question patterns and is not grammatical. “What sounds good to you?” is a natural, low-pressure way to ask someone what food they would enjoy, without demanding a specific choice.
story: My friend and I were deciding what to have for dinner.
We had both had long days and did not feel like cooking.
I asked, “What sounds good to you?”
They mentioned noodles, and I said that sounded good to me too.
We found a place nearby with a short wait.
Over dinner, we talked about plans for the weekend.

bad: I’m looking forward to see you.
good: I’m looking forward to seeing you.
why: “Look forward to” is followed by a noun or an -ing form because “to” is a preposition here, not the infinitive marker. Use “seeing” for an event you are anticipating; the same pattern works in “look forward to hearing from you.”
story: My cousin was visiting our city for a few days.
We had not spent time together since the previous summer.
I sent a message saying, “I’m looking forward to seeing you.”
They replied with their arrival time and flight number.
I offered to meet them at the station after work.
We planned to get dinner near their hotel.

good: Thanks for inviting me.
why: After “for,” use the -ing form “inviting,” not the base verb “invite.” “Thanks for inviting me” is a warm, conversational way to acknowledge an invitation; you can add whether you can attend afterward.
story: A neighbor invited me to a small dinner with a few friends.
I was glad to be included, even though I needed to check my schedule.
I replied, “Thanks for inviting me.”
I looked at my calendar and saw that I was free that evening.
I told them I would be happy to come and asked what I could bring.
They suggested dessert, so I offered to pick something up.

bad: It was nice to meet with you.
good: It was nice meeting you.
why: “Meet with” often suggests a planned meeting or appointment. When saying goodbye after being introduced to someone, “It was nice meeting you” is the usual conversational phrase; “It was nice to meet you” is also natural.
story: I was introduced to a new colleague at a team lunch.
We talked about the neighborhood and a few places to get coffee.
When the lunch ended, I said, “It was nice meeting you.”
They recommended a bakery near the office.
I thanked them and said I might try it on my way home.
We exchanged names again so we could find each other at work.

good: I had a great time.
why: English speakers usually say they “had a good/great time” to describe enjoying an event. “Pass time” means to keep yourself occupied while waiting, so it does not express the same idea.
story: We spent Saturday afternoon at a friend’s backyard barbecue.
People brought different dishes, and everyone shared stories from the week.
As I was leaving, I said, “I had a great time.”
My friend smiled and said they were glad I could make it.
We packed a few leftovers for another guest to take home.
On the way back, I texted the group to thank them again.

bad: Could you tell me how can I get there?
good: Could you tell me how I can get there?
why: After “Could you tell me,” the embedded question uses statement word order: subject before verb (“how I can”). The direct question is “How can I get there?”; when it is inside another question, do not invert the subject and modal a second time.
story: I was planning a walk to a small museum across town.
The map app showed two routes, and I was not sure which entrance was open.
At the information desk, I asked, “Could you tell me how I can get there?”
The staff member pointed out the easiest route and marked it on the map.
I followed the main street until I reached the park.
The museum entrance was just beyond the fountain.

good: Could you pass me the salt, please?
why: “Give me” is direct and can sound like an order at the table. “Pass me” describes moving an item across the table, and “Could you…please?” makes it a courteous request.
story: We were sharing a meal at a small kitchen table.
The salt was beside my friend, just out of my reach.
I asked, “Could you pass me the salt, please?”
They handed it over, and I thanked them.
I seasoned the soup and offered the bread basket in return.
We continued talking while we ate.

good: I appreciate your help.
why: “Appreciate” takes the thing you value as a direct object, so do not put “for” between the verb and “your help.” You can also say “I’m grateful for your help,” where “for” correctly follows the adjective “grateful.”
story: A coworker helped me carry a heavy delivery into the office.
We sorted the boxes before the afternoon meeting began.
I said, “I appreciate your help.”
They told me it was no trouble and asked where the supplies belonged.
We put everything away and cleared the hallway.
The meeting started on time, and I thanked them once more afterward.

good: How was your weekend?
why: Use the simple past “was” when asking for an overall report about a finished weekend. “How was … going?” can work when you are asking about progress during an ongoing period, but it is not the usual question after the weekend has ended.
story: I saw my teammate in the hallway on Monday morning.
We had not talked since Friday afternoon.
I asked, “How was your weekend?”
They told me they visited a nearby town with their family.
I asked what they thought of the food there.
We chatted for a minute before heading to our desks.
